text.tspan: Paul said love is the goal of Christian instruction (1
Tim 1:5). It is the most excellent way (1 Cor 12:31
13:13), the virtue that sums up all other virtues (Col 3:14).
Anyone who loves will possess the other qualities Peter
re lacking in faith and love
and hence are not genuine believers at all.
OR IF THESE QUALITIES ARE YOURS AND ARE INCREASING
Notice the important wording here. “Are yours” and “are increasing.”
The goal is not just to gain these qualities (“are yours”) but to keep
growing in them (“are increasing”). This is the same line of exhortation
Christians are often called to live a
life of continual action and growth. This is because God does not just
want a “one time in my life” kind of people. Relationships are almost
never built on a “one time event.” Instead, they are built, changed, and
oved over a long process of ups and downs
Mayor notes that the word for “increasing” (
in classical writers is a term of disparagement,
implying excess, to be, or to have, more than enough, to
exaggerate. In the N.T. (except in 2 Cor. 8:15…which is
a quotation from Exod. 16:18) it is eulogistic, implying
increase or abundance of what is good
Schreiner also notes about this idea of “increasing,” rightly
means that “we are able to calculate our improvement” of these
, “as if we become five percent more loving each year
. Green rightly states, “There is no excuse for resting content with present attainment. Lack
of spiritual growth is a sign of spiritual death. Nor is there any room for indolence and the
choked by weeds (the cares, riches and pleasures of life) which produces no fruit
The Epistles of Jude and the Second Epistle of St. Peter
